results.title: Problem-Solving Sociology - Virtual Events
results.content: ### May 5, 2026 (in-person in Washington, D.C.) | 09-16:00 EST. ### Problem-solving sociology webinar series 2026. Conveners: Filippo Barbera (University of Torino and Collegio Carlo Alberto) and Monica Prasad (Johns Hopkins University). ### May 15, 2026 | 11-12:00 EST / 17-18:00 CET. "Solving the scapegoat problem in organizations." (Zoom Link). From the perspective of problem-solving sociology, scapegoating represents the opposite of a genuinely problem-oriented approach. While scapegoating closes the problem by locating it in deviant individuals, problem-solving sociology seeks to reopen the analysis at the organizational level, asking how structures, routines, and decision processes made the failure possible. ## Virtual Coffee Hour? The Problem Solving Sociology’s Virtual Coffee Hour is a platform for members to present their work, share their experience, and to connect throughout the year in between ASA conferences. Maurizio Catino is Professor of Sociology of Organizations in the Department of Sociology and Social Research at the University of Milan–Bicocca, Italy, and Visiting Scholar in the Department of Sociology at New York University.

results.title: [PDF] A critical evaluation and research agenda
results.content: The primary source of evidence for the IAH comes from observational (primarily cross-­ sectional) studies that show various self-­ reported measures of individual differences in psy-chological dispositions (e.g., personality traits, psychological needs, moral foundations, etc.) correlate with political attitudes (for instance, Ackermann & Ackermann, 2015; Ackermann & Eckardt, 2023; Choma & Hanoch, 2017; Graham et al., 2009, 2011; Jost, 2017; Jost et al., 2003; Onraet et al., 2011, 2013, 2015; Osborne et al., 2022; Sibley et al., 2012; Thorisdottir et al., 2007; Van Hiel et al., 2016; Wronski et al., 2018; Zmigrod, Ebert, et al., 2021).3 It is beyond the scope of this article to review this literature in detail, but we refer to a relatively recent article in Advances in Political Psychology by Federico and Malka (2018) for a review—and for the most recent reviews, see Bakker (2022); Federico and Malka (2023); Jost (2021), and Osborne et al.
